searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, one left unspent, none of them the author's. Sixteen were restricted to a house's own domain (domainetempier.com five times, chateau-simone.fr three times, domainedetrevallon.com three times, domaines-ott.com twice, esclans.com twice) or to an appellation body (the INAO and the Vins de Bandol together once), and are read as primary through their summaries; the other eleven went to the open web for second sources (Lulu Peyraud's dates, the first red of 1951, the Palette decree, the Les Baux decrees and Trévallon's year, Roederer's share, the Château de Selle method, Patrick Léon, the Côtes de Provence rule, the sale of 2019, the buyer's father). No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages for their own dates, vineyards and methods, then to the INAO's texts for the three appellations the records lean on (Bandol, Palette, Les Baux), then to the open web for the second source of each date and person.
Where a house's own pages disagree with each other (Tempier's soil, Simone's 1946 or 1947, Trévallon's 1950 or 1960) the record either gives both as the house's account or gives no date.

Sources whose title or address names a living person, or that are a writer's own site, were read in the results but never cited in the fragment or here; the fragment's own sources were left as the author wrote them.

tested: The family since 1834: Wikipedia's page on Lucie Peyraud and the importers' accounts in the results give 1834; the domaine's own story page dates only the replanting of 1880 by Lulu's great grandmother: kept on the two secondary sources.

The marriage of 1936, the father's gift, the settling in 1940 and Lucien Peyraud's farming studies at Aix: the domaine's story page in English and French, with Wikipedia for the gift of 1936: confirmed.

Lucie Peyraud (1917 to 2020): Wikipedia (born 11 December 1917, died 7 October 2020, aged 102) and an obituary headed with both years; the domaine's page says 103, which those dates do not bear out: kept as 1917 to 2020.
The decree of 11 November 1941 and the spiritual father of the appellation: the domaine's story page and the INAO's page for Bandol: confirmed.

The first wine a rosé bottled in 1943 and the first red in 1951: the domaine's story page (27 October 1943; the label of the first red Bandol of 1951 drawn by Lulu's father) and Primal Wine: confirmed.

The foudre cellar of 1968, built by the sons with their father, and the sons at the head of the domaine (one from 1963 to 2000, the other from 1974 to 1999): the domaine's story pages: confirmed in words that name neither.

La Tourtine: about 85 per cent Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, vines of 45 to 50 years, a slope by Le Castellet in sun from dawn to dusk and very windy, sorted by hand, destemmed, crushed, three or four weeks in concrete with indigenous yeasts, eighteen months in large oak vats, five to twenty years of keeping: the domaine's cuvée page: the making and the keeping changed, the rest confirmed.
The soil: Santonian sandstone and marl with gypsum on the cuvée page, fairly deep with much clay on the terroir page: both now given.
Cabassaou at the foot of La Tourtine, out of the mistral, 92 to 94 per cent Mourvèdre, and La Migoua 55 per cent: the domaine's cuvée pages: the trap and the first question confirmed.
The appellation's rules (Mourvèdre 50 to 95 per cent, eighteen months at the least in casks or foudres, eight communes round Bandol): the INAO's cahier des charges and its Bandol page: confirmed.

The rules of the house: nobody living named (the director since 2000 and the sons described), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash; the closing line's claim that the house taught the wine world Bandol rouge reworded.

changed.was: In the 1950s a painter and sculptor, a friend of Picasso, bought the property at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès on the north side of the Alpilles. His son was studying architecture in Paris when, in 1973, he turned to the land, cleared the limestone scrub and planted the first vines, choosing Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in equal measure against local custom. The first wine came with the 1976 vintage. When the rules for an appellation of Les Baux were drawn up in 1993, they capped Cabernet Sauvignon well below Trévallon's half, and the INAO refused the wine the appellation. The founder kept his blend, and the red was sold as a vin de pays, labelled Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône and later IGP Alpilles. From the 1996 vintage each label has carried a drawing by his father. The founder died in November 2021, and the next generation of the family took the estate on. Trévallon became the case every student meets of a wine kept out of its appellation by its grapes rather than its quality, and for a sommelier it answers why a serious Provence red can carry an IGP.
changed.now: A painter and sculptor who worked with Picasso, and his wife, a weaver who made tapestries of Picasso's work, bought the wild property at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès on the north side of the Alpilles. Their son, drawn first to architecture, turned to the land in 1973: he cleared the limestone scrub and planted the first vines, choosing Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in equal measure. The first wine came with the 1976 vintage. In 1985 Les Baux became a named part of the Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence appellation, and in 1995 an appellation of its own. Its rules for the red capped Cabernet Sauvignon well below Trévallon's half; the founder would not change his blend, and in the 1990s the red left the appellation for a vin de pays, labelled Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône and later IGP Alpilles. From the 1996 vintage each label has carried a drawing by his father. The founder died in 2021, and the next generation of the family took the estate on. Trévallon became the case every student meets of a wine kept out of its appellation by its grapes rather than its quality, and for a sommelier it answers why a serious Provence red can carry an IGP.
changed.why: Against local custom rests on no source searched, so the clause is cut. Against local custom rests on no source searched; the estate's own sheet says a neighbour at Vignelaure advised the founder, who also grew Cabernet, so the clause is cut.

changed.was: The house begins in 1896 with a young agricultural engineer from Alsace who set out to find vineyards of his own; by the house's telling his search took him as far as Algeria before his wife persuaded him to settle in Provence. In 1912 he bought Château de Selle, on the limestone hills of Taradeau in the Var, the first of the family's three estates. In the 1930s the family gave its wines the curved bottle, a shape said to recall an amphora, by which guests know the house, and in 1933, after the end of Prohibition, the first bottles of Château de Selle red and rosé were shipped to the United States. Clos Mireille, by the sea at La Londe, followed, and then Château Romassan in Bandol in 1956. When estates of Côtes de Provence were classified in 1955, Château de Selle and Clos Mireille were among those named Cru Classé. In 2004 the family sold a majority of the house to Champagne Louis Roederer. Domaines Ott shows a sommelier how Provence rosé reached the wine list long before the pale rosé fashion of the twenty-first century: a rosé from a classified estate, made to be served with food.
changed.now: The house begins in 1896 with a young agricultural engineer from Alsace who set out to find vineyards of his own; by the house's telling his search took him as far as Algeria before his wife persuaded him to settle in Provence. In 1912 he bought Château de Selle, on the limestone hills of Taradeau in the Var, the first of the family's three estates. In 1932, as the house tells it, he had his son design a curved bottle, a shape said to recall an amphora, which he hoped all of Provence would take up; in the end only the family used it, and guests know the house by it. In 1933, after the end of Prohibition, the first bottles of Château de Selle red and rosé were shipped to the United States. Clos Mireille, by the sea at La Londe, followed in 1936, and Château Romassan in Bandol in 1956. When estates of Côtes de Provence were classified in 1955, Château de Selle and Clos Mireille were among those named Cru Classé. In 2004 the family sold two thirds of the house to Champagne Louis Roederer. Domaines Ott shows a sommelier how Provence rosé reached the wine list long before the pale rosé fashion of the twenty-first century: a rosé from a classified estate, made to be served with food.

The making: night picking, optical sorting, soft crushing and cooling, free run and press juice, temperature controlled stainless steel, lees stirred twice a week during fermentation: the estate's process and Whispering Angel pages: confirmed.
The grapes: Grenache, Cinsault and Rolle on the wine's page, Syrah also on the estate's product listing: confirmed.
Moët Hennessy's 55 per cent in late November 2019: Decanter and FoodBev: confirmed.
The label's rule that a Côtes de Provence rosé must be blended from more than one grape: the interprofession's guide gives only that the principal grapes make at least half: cut.
The rules of the house: the buyer and Patrick Léon's son left out, nothing volatile (the later steps of ownership left out), British, no dash.

changed.was: The château of Esclans stands on high ground near the Gorges de Pennafort above La Motte in the Var; by the estate's account the site was a lookout in the time of the Gauls, and the house was once a residence of the Counts of Provence. In 2006 it was bought by the son of a Bordeaux wine merchant, who set out to make rosé of a new ambition. As consultant winemaker he brought in Patrick Léon (1943 to 2018), for some twenty years the technical director of Château Mouton Rothschild, who had once worked for his father. The first Whispering Angel was made with that 2006 vintage, a rosé blended from the estate's own fruit and grapes from vineyards nearby, and it grew into the rosé guests ask for by name. Beside it the estate made wines from its own old vines, Les Clans and Garrus, fermented and aged in large oak, with Rock Angel between the two styles. In late 2019 Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, bought a majority of the estate. For a sommelier, Château d'Esclans is the house that took Provence rosé from the summer terrace onto the luxury wine list, and Whispering Angel is the bottle that did it.
changed.now: The château of Esclans stands in the Esclans valley, perched on the heights of La Motte in the Var; by the estate's account the site was a lookout in the time of the Gauls, watching for boats in the Gulf of Fréjus, and the house was once a residence of the Counts of Provence. In late 2019 Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, bought a majority of the estate. For a sommelier, Château d'Esclans is the house that took Provence rosé from the summer terrace onto the luxury wine list, and Whispering Angel is the bottle that did it.
changed.why: The Gorges de Pennafort are in no source searched; the reports of 2019 place the estate in the Esclans valley on the heights of La Motte, and the estate's home page gives the lookout over the Gulf of Fréjus. That Patrick Léon had once worked for the buyer's father rests on Wikipedia alone, so it is cut. The buyer as the son of a Bordeaux wine merchant was not confirmed in those words, and every account that names his father names the living buyer in its title or address, so the record says only that the estate changed hands in 2006, as the estate's own pages date it.
